title: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap
field: AI 研发 · 模型训练

design_key.question: 预训练数据规模（预训练 token 预算）如何影响 Muon 与 AdamW 预训练模型在微调中的学习–遗忘权衡差距？标题称这一差距会随数据规模反转。具体问题是：在不同模型规模和数据预算下，哪种预训练优化器能得到更好的学习–遗忘前沿？差距从哪个预算开始转为正值（crossover）？
independent: 预训练优化器：AdamW vs Muon。Muon 只更新隐藏层权重矩阵，embedding、输出层和 norm 仍由 AdamW 更新。
预训练数据预算：150M 至 154B 个 DCLM token。crossover 以 TPR 表示，摘录未给出 TPR 的定义。
模型规模：OLMo 风格，30M–600M 参数。
预训练超参数的选取方式：(1) lowest-pretraining-loss 设定，每个优化器按最小预训练损失调参；(2) best-frontier 设定，遍历全部预训练与微调配置，取最优学习–遗忘前沿。
微调学习率扫描：AdamW 为 1e-4 至 1e-2，Muon 为 6e-4 至 2e-2。用于覆盖完整的学习–遗忘谱。
预训练超参数扫描（best-frontier 设定）：摘录称范围很广，细节见附录 C，摘录未给出具体取值。
微调阶段的优化器与预训练优化器如何配对：摘录未给出。
dependent: 学习：每个微调 checkpoint 在 held-out 微调数据上的微调损失。
遗忘：每个微调 checkpoint 在 held-out 预训练（DCLM）数据上的预训练损失。
学习–遗忘前沿：由所有微调运行在上述两种损失构成的平面中拟合得到。
微调差距 G_FT：沿 AdamW 前沿按弧长均匀采样 100 个点，取每点到 Muon 前沿最近点的欧氏距离；若该 AdamW 点更靠近原点，距离取负。G_FT 的完整定义在第 2 节，摘录未给出最终的聚合方式。
Crossover TPR：G_FT > 0 时对应的最小数据预算。
baselines: AdamW 预训练模型，作为与 Muon 对比的标准优化器。
lowest-pretraining-loss 设定：即常规的、按最小预训练损失选取模型的做法，与 best-frontier 设定对照。
摘录未给出其他外部基线方法。
data: 微调：GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021)、StackMathQA (Zhang, 2024)、Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023)、MusicPile (Yuan et al., 2024)。
评估：上述微调数据的 held-out 部分，以及 DCLM 预训练数据的 held-out 部分。
数据划分比例与具体样本量：摘录未给出。
design_key.scale: 模型为 OLMo 风格，参数量 30M–600M。预训练 token 预算为 150M–154B（DCLM），序列长度 4096，全局 batch 为 2^20 token。学习率调度为 WSD，weight decay 0.1，梯度裁剪 1.0；AdamW 取 (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.98)。具体的模型规模档位、数据预算档位、扫描点数、总运行数和计算开销：摘录未给出。

method_excerpt:
Pretraining. We pretrain OLMo-style 30M–600M models on 150 M to 154 B DCLM tokens, comparing AdamW and Muon under a warmup–stable–decay (WSD) schedule. We sweep hyperparameters broadly and report the complete pretraining methodology in Appendix C.
Fine-tuning. For each base model, we evaluate the learning–forgetting tradeoff on four standard datasets: GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), StackMathQA (Zhang, 2024), Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023), and MusicPile (Yuan et al., 2024), sweeping AdamW learning rates from 10^{-4} to 10^{-2} and Muon learning rates from 6\times 10^{-4} to 2\times 10^{-2} (Section C.2). [...] We then plot the learning–forgetting frontier over the resulting runs. We choose a broad learning-rate range to ensure we capture the complete learning–forgetting tradeoff spectrum: higher learning rates favor learning at the expense of forgetting, while lower rates preserve pretraining knowledge but learn less.
Evaluating the learning–forgetting tradeoff. For each fine-tuned checkpoint, we compute the fine-tuning loss and pretraining loss on held-out fine-tuning and pretraining (DCLM) data, and use these checkpoints to approximate the learning–forgetting tradeoff. [...] We evaluate the learning–forgetting tradeoff in two settings: lowest-pretraining-loss setting, and the best-frontier setting.
1. Lowest-pretraining-loss setting: Pretraining hyperparameters are typically selected to minimize pretraining loss. Therefore, for each optimizer, we tune the pretraining hyperparameters to minimize pretraining loss for a given pretraining data budget and model size. We then sweep across all fine-tuning configurations for each of the lowest-loss pretrained models, and evaluate the resulting frontier.
2. Best-frontier setting: However, prior studies find that the lowest-loss pretrained model is not always the best model after fine-tuning: models pretrained with other hyperparameters can offer a better learning–forgetting tradeoff (Watts et al., 2026). Therefore, for each pretraining optimizer, we additionally sweep across all pretraining and fine-tuning configurations to achieve the best possible learning–forgetting frontier for a given pretraining data budget and model size (Section C.1.3).
Optimization. Every model is pretrained with sequence length 4096 , a global batch of 2^{20} tokens, a warmup–stable–decay (WSD) schedule, weight decay 0.1 and gradient clipping at 1.0 . AdamW uses (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.98) . Muon updates the hidden weight matrices; the remaining parameters (embeddings, output layer and norms) are updated by AdamW.
Fine-tuning gap and crossover. We estimate the fine-tuning gap G_{\mathrm{FT}} of Section 2 from 100 points sampled uniformly by arc length along the AdamW frontier, each assigned its Euclidean distance to the nearest point of the Muon frontier, negative when that point lies closer to the origin. The crossover TPR is the smallest budget at which G_{\mathrm{FT}}>0 .
blind_brief:
研究问题：近来 Muon 在大语言模型预训练中常被报告比 AdamW 更快降低预训练损失。但实际部署的模型几乎都要经过微调，真正重要的是学习–遗忘权衡：模型既要学会目标任务，又要保住预训练知识。本研究要回答的是：Muon 在预训练阶段的优势，能否延续到微调后的这一权衡上？这种比较又如何随预训练数据量和模型规模变化？

为什么值得做：业界通常按预训练损失挑选优化器和超参。如果预训练损失不能很好地代表模型的可适应性，这种做法就需要重新审视。

实验设计：用 AdamW 和 Muon 分别预训练 OLMo 风格的 30M–600M 模型，在 DCLM 上覆盖从很少到远超计算最优的数据量（以每参数 token 数 TPR 计）。每个基座模型在数学、指令跟随、音乐四个数据集上微调，并大范围扫描微调优化器和学习率。以微调集损失衡量学习，以留出预训练数据损失衡量遗忘，取帕累托前沿，并用带符号的前沿距离（fine-tuning gap）比较两种优化器。基座模型的选取分两种：只取预训练损失最低的模型，或在多组预训练超参中取最佳前沿。另设 replay、EWC 等微调正则作为稳健性检验。机制层面，作者提出一个基于输出 logit 的鲁棒性指标，并在高斯线性联想记忆模型中对比 GD 与 Muon，做单步理论推导和多步仿真，同时用高斯权重扰动作为辅助探针。

review_excerpt:
Main result: Pretraining data scale reverses the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap. We compare the fine-tuning gap for AdamW and Muon at different pretraining data budgets in the lowest-pretraining-loss setting, using StackMathQA as the fine-tuning dataset (Figure 3a). At small pretraining data budgets ( 9.6 B tokens), Muon Pareto-dominates AdamW (Figure 1) and the fine-tuning gap is negative. At larger pretraining data budgets, this trend reverses: beyond 2.4 B tokens, AdamW achieves lower fine-tuning loss with less forgetting than Muon. The trend also holds in the best-frontier setting (Figure 12), and for additional fine-tuning datasets in Appendix D.
As model size scales, AdamW surpasses Muon at progressively smaller data budgets. We find that the crossover TPR decreases with model size. On StackMathQA, the crossover is 320 TPR for 30M models but only 10 TPR for 600M models (Figure 2). The specific crossover TPR depends on the fine-tuning dataset, but the broader trend persists; as model size grows, the crossover TPR decreases, and Muon’s advantage reverses with substantially smaller data budgets.
We hypothesize that in the lowest-pretraining-loss setting, this scaling trend is driven by two factors: Muon’s shrinking pretraining loss advantage and increased degradation relative to AdamW (Figure 3b,c). For each optimizer and model size, we compare its base pretraining loss and its degradation \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{FT}})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}}) , after fine-tuning on StackMathQA. First, for a fixed TPR, the gap in pretraining loss between Muon and AdamW shrinks as model size increases, reducing Muon’s advantage as a lower-loss base model. Additionally, for a fixed TPR and fine-tuning loss, Muon forgets increasingly more than AdamW as model size grows. Consequently, as model size scales, Muon’s pretraining advantage over AdamW narrows, while its forgetting relative to AdamW increases, enabling AdamW to overtake Muon at progressively smaller data budgets. This establishes that Muon’s orthogonalized update causally induces forgetting, and the reversal will therefore hold at every model scale and for every fine-tuning distribution.
Setup. Springer et al. (2025) show that adding isotropic Gaussian noise to pretrained weights reproduces key empirical trends in forgetting after fine-tuning. Motivated by this connection, we study Gaussian weight perturbations as a simpler setting in which to investigate why the learning–forgetting gap between Muon and AdamW changes with pretraining budget. At the same checkpoints as in Section 3, we add isotropic Gaussian noise to each weight matrix, scaled to a fraction \delta of the matrix’s norm, and measure the loss increase \Delta_{\mathrm{noise}}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}};\delta):=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\widetilde{\theta}_{\delta})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}}) , where \widetilde{\theta}_{\delta} denotes the perturbed weights; a smaller increase indicates greater perturbation robustness. See Section E.2 for full experimental details.
Language models. We measure MSR as in Section 4.3 and degradation by the held-out loss increase of Section B.1.1. The robustness threshold \delta^{\ast} is the perturbation magnitude at which this increase reaches \Delta L nats. Across checkpoints, \rho and \delta^{\ast} are strongly correlated for both \Delta L=0.05 and 0.1 (Figure 7b): the Spearman correlation over the 72 checkpoints is +0.83 at both thresholds, and within each optimizer it is +0.87 to +0.89 for AdamW and +0.92 to +0.93 for Muon. Full experimental details appear in Section E.3.
Springer et al. (2025) and Zhou & Kumar (2024) show that adding isotropic Gaussian noise to pretrained weights reproduces key empirical trends in forgetting after fine-tuning. [伪造文献：Zhou, H. & Kumar, R. (2024). Gaussian Weight Noise as a Proxy for Catastrophic Forgetting in Language Models.]
